title: Job 38:31–41
context: In this speech the LORD turns to the stars, the laws of the heavens, the clouds and lightning, the wisdom placed within creatures, and then to the feeding of the lioness and the raven. The identifications of the star groups named in 38:31-32 are traditional but uncertain. The section moves from the heavens to the animal world, which the speech continues in chapter 39. Both traditions read it as shared ground on God’s wise and generous rule over all he has made, including creatures far from human care.

verses.text: “Can you bind the cluster of the Pleiades, or loosen the cords of Orion?
verses.arminianNotes: Can you bind the cluster of the Pleiades, or loosen the cords of Orion? Arminian readers note that the same names appear in Job 9:9 and Amos 5:8; the identifications are traditional, and the exact star groups are uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD asking whether Job can control the heavens, as Job himself had confessed God made these stars (9:9). The images of binding and loosening are poetic.

verses.text: Can you lead the constellations out in their season? Or can you guide the Bear with her cubs?
verses.arminianNotes: Can you lead the constellations out in their season? Or can you guide the Bear with her cubs? Arminian readers note that the word rendered the constellations is understood in several ways, and some translations leave it as a name, Mazzaroth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identifications loosely, including the Bear. The point is that the stars move in their seasons at God’s direction, not at Job’s command.

verses.text: Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you establish its dominion over the earth?
verses.arminianNotes: Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you establish its dominion over the earth? Arminian readers see order in the sky as a reflection of God’s faithful governance of creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the laws of the heavens suggest a fixed order set by God. The verse makes no scientific claim; it stresses that Job neither set nor controls that order.

verses.text: “Can you lift up your voice to the clouds, that abundance of waters may cover you?
verses.arminianNotes: Can you lift up your voice to the clouds, that abundance of waters may cover you? Arminian readers see a question exposing human helplessness before the forces of weather.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that only God’s voice commands the clouds. The contrast highlights the gap between divine authority and human words, which had been many in the dialogue.

verses.text: Can you send out lightnings, that they may go? Do they report to you, ‘Here we are’?
verses.arminianNotes: Can you send out lightnings, that they may go? Do they report to you, ‘Here we are’? Arminian readers see lightning pictured as servants answering a master’s call, a call only God can make.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the personification of lightning as obedient messengers. Every element of creation answers to God, and none of it reports to Job, however eloquent his words.

verses.text: Who has put wisdom in the inward parts? Or who has given understanding to the mind?
verses.arminianNotes: Who has put wisdom in the inward parts? Or who has given understanding to the mind? Arminian readers see wisdom as a gift God places within his creatures, including the capacity Job has used in his arguments.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Hebrew words here are uncertain, and some translations render them as birds rather than as the inner self. Either way, wisdom is presented as God’s gift.

verses.text: Who can count the clouds by wisdom? Or who can pour out the containers of the sky,
verses.arminianNotes: Who can count the clouds by wisdom? Or who can pour out the containers of the sky? Arminian readers see God’s knowledge extending to every cloud, a care beyond human counting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the containers of the sky continue the poetic picture of rain stored above. God alone has the wisdom to number and release them.

verses.text: when the dust runs into a mass, and the clods of earth stick together?
verses.arminianNotes: When the dust runs into a mass, and the clods of earth stick together? Arminian readers see the effect of rain on dry ground, turning dust into soil, a small wonder of daily providence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse completes the thought of the previous one: God’s rain binds the earth together. The imagery is agricultural and poetic.

verses.text: “Can you hunt the prey for the lioness, or satisfy the appetite of the young lions,
verses.arminianNotes: Can you hunt the prey for the lioness, or satisfy the appetite of the young lions? Arminian readers see the LORD turning from the heavens to the animal world, where his care continues.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Psalm 104:21 likewise speaks of young lions seeking their food from God. Both passages show that God provides even for fierce creatures.

verses.text: when they crouch in their dens, and lie in wait in the thicket?
verses.arminianNotes: When they crouch in their dens, and lie in wait in the thicket? Arminian readers see the hidden life of wild animals, known to God though unseen by people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the details of crouching and waiting picture the lion’s natural ways. God governs and sustains these creatures in their own habitats.

verses.text: Who provides for the raven his prey, when his young ones cry to God, and wander for lack of food?
verses.arminianNotes: Who provides for the raven his prey, when his young ones cry to God? Arminian readers see God hearing the cries of even small and unloved creatures, and they note Jesus’ use of the ravens in Luke 12:24.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Psalm 147:9 likewise speaks of God feeding the young ravens. The chapter ends with God’s care for creatures, still without explaining Job’s suffering, as the speech continues in chapter 39.
